title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    A superalgebra is a vector superspace $V=V_{\bar0} \oplus V_{\bar1}$ endowed with a bilinear multiplication $\ \cdot \ $ that satisfies $V_{i} \cdot V_{j} \subseteq V_{i + j \bmod 2}$, $i, j \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

\normalfont
    If $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie superalgebra, then a $\mathfrak{g}$\textit{-module} is a vector space $V$ together with a bilinear map $\mathfrak{g} \times V \to V, \ (a, v) \mapsto av$ satisfying
    \[
       [a, b]v = a(bv) - (-1)^{\abs{a} \abs{b}}b(av),
    \relax
    \ifmmode

    for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $v \in V$.

name: $\mathfrak{g}$-module

title: Example
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a Lie superalgebra. Then, the space of all endomorphisms of $\mathfrak{g}$, $\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})$, is clearly associative, and is thus a Lie superalgebra by Example \ref{example-assoc-superalgebra}. Now define the \textit{adjoint representation} of $\mathfrak{g}$ by $\mathrm{ad} \colon \mathfrak{g} \to \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})$ such that 
    \[
        \mathrm{ad}_a(b)=[a, b], \quad \forall a, b \in \mathfrak{g}.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    We notice that $\mathrm{ad}$ is a homomorphism of Lie superalgebras due to the Super Jacobi identity of Definition \ref{def-lie-super}. Moreover, the resulting action $\mathrm{ad}_a$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ onto itself is called the \textit{adjoint action}, similar to the adjoint module of a Lie algebra.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The even part of $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra on its own. This is because, by the $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-grading, we have closure under the Lie superbracket; that is, $[\mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}, \mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}] \subset \mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}$. Thus, in $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}$, the superbracket reduces to the Lie bracket. This is not true for the odd part $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar1}$ as closure is not satisfied: $[\mathfrak{g}_{\bar1}, \mathfrak{g}_{\bar1}] \subset \mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}$. Under the adjoint action, $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar1}$ is actually a $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar0}$-module. For more details, see N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{cheng}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\bar0} \oplus \mathcal{A}_{\bar1}$ be a superalgebra. Then a linear endomorphism $D \in \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})_s$ such that $s \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is called a superderivation of $\mathcal{A}$ of degree $s$ if 
    \[
        D(ab)=D(a)b +(-1)^{s \abs{a}}aD(b), \quad \forall a, b \in \mathcal{A}.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    Let $\mathrm{Der}(\mathcal{A})_s$ denote the space of derivations on $\mathcal{A}$ of degree $s$. If $s = \bar0$, the subspace $\mathrm{Der}_{\bar0}(\mathcal{A})$ consists of all even derivations, meaning that $D(\mathcal{A}_s) \subset \mathcal{A}_s$ for $s \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Conversely, if $s = \bar1$, the subspace $\mathrm{Der}_{\bar1}(\mathcal{A})$ consists of all odd derivations, implying $D(\mathcal{A}_s) \subset \mathcal{A}_{s+1 \bmod 2}$ for $s \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Hence, the superspace of superderivations of $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathrm{Der}(\mathcal{A}) = \mathrm{Der}(\mathcal{A})_{\bar0} \oplus \mathrm{Der}(\mathcal{A})_{\bar1}$ is called the \textit{Lie superalgebra of superderivations of $\mathcal{A}$} and is a subalgebra of the Lie superalgebra $\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{A})$ paired with the superbracket operator. For more details on superderivations, see N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{musson, cheng}.
head: environment
name: Superderivations

title: Example
body_md:
\normalfont
    Take the adjoint action. If $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie superalgebra, then similarly to Example 2.1, through the super Jacobi identity, $\mathrm{ad \ \mathfrak{g} \in \mathrm{Der}(\mathfrak{g})}$. That is, $\mathrm{ad}_a$ is a superderivation, for all $a \in \mathfrak{g}$. These are called the \textit{inner derivations}, and they form an ideal in $\mathrm{Der}(\mathfrak{g})$.
head: environment

label: blockmat
title: Example
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $V=V_{\bar0} \oplus V_{\bar1} \cong \mathbb{C}^{m \mid n}$ be a vector superspace with $\mathrm{sdim}=m \mid n$ such that $\mathrm{End}(V)$ is an associative superalgebra. By Example \ref{example-assoc-superalgebra}, equipping $\mathrm{End}(V)$ with the Lie superbracket (in this case called the \textit{supercommutator}) transforms it into a Lie superalgebra called the \textbf{general linear Lie superalgebra} and is denoted by $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ or, in this case, by $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$. By fixing a basis, $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$ can be realized as the set of all $(m +n) \times (m +n)$ block matrices of the form 
    \begin{equation}
        X = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D\end{pmatrix}
        \relax{blockmat},
    \end{equation}

    \noindent
    where $A, B, C,$ and $D$ are matrices respectively of the form $m \times m, \ m \times n, \ n \times m,$ and $n \times n$. The even subalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)_{\bar{0}}$ consists of all matrices in the form of Eq. \eqref{blockmat} such that $B= C = O$, while the odd subalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)_{\bar{1}}$ consists of all matrices of the form in Eq. \eqref{blockmat} with $A= D = O$. 

    Define the \textit{supertrace} of $X$ by 
    \[
        \mathrm{str}(X) = \mathrm{tr}(A) - \mathrm{tr}(D),
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    \noindent 
    where $\mathrm{tr}$ denotes the usual  trace of a square matrix. 

    One can check that for any $X, Y \in \mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$, we have $\mathrm{str([X, Y])=0}$ due to the cyclic property of the supertrace operator. See N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{cheng, musson} for more details.
    
    The subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$ consisting of all matrices in the form of Eq. \eqref{blockmat} with supertrace zero is called the \textbf{special linear Lie superalgebra} and is denoted by $\mathfrak{sl}(m|n)$. By using the cyclic property of the supertrace and the fact that $\mathfrak{sl}(m|n)$ is spanned by commutators $[X, Y] \in \mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$, we can show $[\mathfrak{gl}(m|n), \mathfrak{gl}(m|n)] = \mathfrak{sl}(m|n)$.

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $\mathbb{K}$. A \textit{bilinear form} is a bilinear map $\mathscr{B} \colon V \times V \to \mathbb{K}$ such that for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{K}$, the following are satisfied

    \begin{enumerate}
        \setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}                        
        \setlength{\parskip}{0pt}                                      
        \setlength{\topsep}{0pt}
        \@par\hangindent 2em [(i)] $\mathscr{B}(\alpha u +\beta v, w)= \alpha \mathscr{B}(u, w) + \beta \mathscr{B}(v, w)$,
        \@par\hangindent 2em [(ii)] $\mathscr{B}(u, \alpha v +\beta w)= \alpha \mathscr{B}(u, w) + \beta \mathscr{B}(v, w)$.
    \end{enumerate}

    Let $\mathscr{B}$ be a bilinear form. Then, $\mathscr{B}$ is said to be \textit{symmetric} if $\mathscr{B}(u, v)=\mathscr{B}(v, u)$ for all $u, v \in V$. $\mathscr{B}$ is said to be \textit{antisymmetric} if $\mathscr{B}(u, v)=-\mathscr{B}(v,u)$ for all $u, v \in V$. Moreover, $\mathscr{B}$ is called \textit{alternating} if $\mathscr{B}(u, u)=0$ for all $u \in V$. 

    Relevant to this paper, a bilinear form $\mathscr{B}$ is called \textit{nondegenerate} if for every $v \in V$ with $v \neq 0$, there exists $u \in V$ such that 
    \[
        \mathscr{B}(u, v) \not= 0. 
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
head: environment
name: Bilinear form

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $\mathscr{B}$ be a nondegenerate, even bilinear form on a vector superspace $V$ that is either supersymmetric or anti-supersymmetric. Then, $\mathfrak{osp}(V, \mathscr{B})$ denotes the \textit{orthosymplectic Lie superalgebra} preserving the bilinear form $\mathscr{B}$ and is defined by
    \[
       \mathfrak{osp}(V, \mathscr{B}) = \{X \in \mathfrak{gl}(V) \mid \mathscr{B}(X(v), w) + (-1)^{|X||v|} \mathscr{B}(v, X(w)) = 0 , \forall v,w \in V\}.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    
    We can also define this Lie superalgebra in matrix form. Fix a homogeneous basis for the superspace $V = V_{\bar{0}} \oplus V_{\bar{1}}$ with $\mathrm{dim}(V_{\bar{0}}) = m$ and $\mathrm{dim}(V_{\bar{1}}) = n$ identifying the isomorphism $V \cong \mathbb{K}^{m|n}$. Let
    \[
        J = \begin{pmatrix} G & O \\ O & H \end{pmatrix}
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    \noindent
    be the matrix representing $\mathscr{B}$ in block form such that $G$ is an $m \times m$ matrix and $H$ is an $n \times n$ matrix; additionally, $G$ is symmetric while $H$ is antisymmetric. A block matrix $X \in \mathfrak{gl}(m | n)$ in the form of Eq. \eqref{blockmat} lies in $\mathfrak{osp}(V, \mathscr{B}) = \mathfrak{osp}(m|n)$ if 
    \[
        A^{T}G + GA= B^{T}G - HC = D^{T}H + HD = 0.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    For more details on  orthosymplectic Lie algebras, see N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{scheunert, musson}.
    
    The Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2) = \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar0} \oplus \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar1}$ is a classical Lie superalgebra of superdimension $3|2$, defined as the subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}(1|2)$ preserving a non-degenerate even supersymmetric bilinear form $\mathscr{B}$ on the superspace $\mathbb{K}^{1|2}$. Concretely, we have that
    \[
        \mathfrak{osp}(1|2) = \{ X \in \mathfrak{gl}(1|2) \mid \mathscr{B}(Xv, w) + (-1)^{|X||v|} \mathscr{B}(v, Xw) = 0, \forall v,w \in \mathbb{K}^{1|2} \}.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    \noindent
    We can take $\mathscr{B}$ to be represented by the matrix

    \begin{equation}
        J = 
        \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
        0 & -1 & 0
        \end{pmatrix},  
        \relax{biformmat}
    \end{equation}

    \noindent
    with respect to a homogeneous basis, where $G=1$ and $H= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then
    \[
        \mathfrak{osp}(1|2) = \{ X \in \mathfrak{gl}(1|2) \mid X^\text{sT}J + JX = 0 \},
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    where \(X^\text{sT}\) denotes the supertranspose of $X$. If $X$ is in the form of Eq. \eqref{blockmat}, then 

    \[
        X^{sT} = \begin{pmatrix} A^T & C^T \\ -B^T & D^T \end{pmatrix}.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    
    Explicitly, the even part $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar0} \cong \mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{K})$, and the odd part $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar1}$ transforms to a 2-dimensional module under the adjoint action of \(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{K})\). Thus,
    \begin{equation}
        \mathfrak{osp}(1|2) = \mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{K}) \oplus \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar1}.
        \relax{osp12}
    \end{equation}

    \noindent
    This isomorphism is exceptional and only true for $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$.
    This makes $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$ a natural example of a simple Lie superalgebra, with tractable structure and close connections to Lie algebras. In particular, the isomorphism $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar 0} \cong \mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{K})$ implies that the (bosonic) generators span the even part
    \begin{equation}
        \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar{0}} = \Biggl\langle E = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \ F = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \ H = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \Biggr\rangle.
        \relax{evengen}
    \end{equation} 

    \noindent
    These are called the \textit{even generators}, and they satisfy the following commutation relations 
    \begin{equation}
    \relax{sl2-relations}
    [H, E]=2E, \ [H,F] = -2F, \ \mathrm{and} \ [E,F] = H. 
    \end{equation}
    \noindent
    This also implies that $\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar{0}}) = \mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{K}))=3$.
    
    It is important not to confuse the matrix $H$ in Eq. \eqref{biformmat} with that of Eq. \eqref{evengen}.
    
    Similarly, the (fermionic) generators span the odd part $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar1}$
    
    \begin{equation}
        \mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar{1}} = \Biggl\langle T_{+} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \ T_{-} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \Biggr\rangle. \relax{oddgen}
    \end{equation}

    \noindent
    These are called the \textit{odd generators} and, by their parity, they satisfy the following anticommutation relations:
    \begin{equation}
        \{T_{+}, T_{+}\} = 2E, \ \{T_{+}, T_{-}\} = \{T_{-}, T_{+}\} = H, \ \{T_{-}, T_{-}\} = -2F. \relax{odd_rela}
    \end{equation}

    Now, considering the odd-even relations:
    \begin{equation}
        [T_{+}, E] = [T_{-}, F] = 0, \ [T_{+}, F] = [T_{-}, H] = T_{-}, \ [T_{+}, H] = -T_{+}, \ [T_{-}, E] = T_{+}. \relax{even_odd_rela}
    \end{equation}

    Thus, $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$ is said to have a (graded) basis denoted by $\langle E,F,H \mid T_{+}, T_{-}\rangle$.
    
    \begin{remark}
        In physics, a normalization of $\pm \frac{1}{2}$ is applied to the commutation relations with $H$ to assign a spin to odd generators. In mathematics, a normalization of $2$ is assigned as a result of the even subalgebra relations involving $H$. See N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{mnev}. 
    \end{remark}

title: Proof
body_md:
We can verify the Lie algebra axioms. The product $[a, b]$ is trivially linear in $a$ and $b$. Moreover, we can see that $[a, a]=0$. Lastly, for all $a, b, c \in \mathcal{A}$, we check the Jacobi identity
\begin{align*}
    [a, [b, c]] &=  a(bc - cb) - (bc - cb)a \\
                &= a(bc) - a(cb) - (bc)a + (cb)a.
\end{align*}

\noindent
We obtain similar expressions for $[c, [a, b]]$ and $[b, [c, a]]$ such that
\begin{align*}
        [a, [b, c]] + [c, [a, b]] + [b, [c, a]] &= a(bc) - a(cb) - (bc)a + (cb)a \\ & \quad + c(ab) - c(ba) - (ab)c + (ba)c \\ & \quad + b(ca) - b(ac) - (ca)b + (ac)b.
\end{align*}

Now, knowing $\mathcal{A}$ is a left-symmetric algebra, using the symmetry identity, we see $(a, b, c) = (b, a, c)$, $(b, c, a) = (c, b, a)$, and $(c, a, b) = (a, c, b)$. Thus

    \[
        [a, [b, c]] + [c, [a, b]] + [b, [c, a]] = 0.
  \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

label: nullstellensatz
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be an algebraically closed field and let $I \subset \mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ be an ideal. Then,
$V(I) = \varnothing$ if and only if $I = \langle 1 \rangle$. \relax{nullstellensatz}

label: example1-term-order
title: Example
body_md:
\relax{example1-term-order}
    \normalfont
    Fix a lex term order. Consider the polynomial ring $\mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, x_3]$ and the monomials $x_{1}^2x_{2}$ and $x_{1}x_{2}^{3}x_{3}^{2}$. We see that $x_{1}^2x_{2} \succ x_{1}x_{2}^{3}x_{3}^{2}$ as 
    \[
      \boldsymbol{\alpha} - \boldsymbol{\beta} = (2,1,0) - (1,3,2) = (1,-2,-2).  
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    \noindent
    The leftmost nonzero entry $(\boldsymbol{\alpha} - \boldsymbol{\beta})_{1} = 1$ is clearly positive.
    
    In the polynomial ring $\mathbb{K}[x_{1}, x_{2}]$, we have 
    \[
        \cdots \succ x_{1}^{2} \succ \cdots \succ x_{1}x_{2}^{2} \succ x_{1}x_{2} \succ x_{1} \succ \cdots \succ x_{2}^{3} \succ x_{2}^{2} \succ x_{2} \succ 1.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

       \boldsymbol{\alpha} - \boldsymbol{\beta} = (2,1,1) - (1,3,0) = (1,-2, 1).

    Fix a deglex term order. Consider the same polynomial ring and monomials as in Example \ref{example1-term-order}. We see that

        |\boldsymbol{\alpha}| - |\boldsymbol{\beta}| = 3 - 6 = -3.

    \[f(x) = \sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}x^{k} = a_{0} + a_{1}x + \cdots + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + a_{n}x^{n} \in \mathbb{K}[x],\relax

title: Example
body_md:
\normalfont
    For the multivariate case, these notions differ. We must first fix a term order before defining these concepts. Let $\succ$ be a term order. Consider a nonzero multivariate polynomial given by 
    \[
        g({\mathbf{x}}) = \sum\limits_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} a_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \in \mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], 
    \relax
    \ifmmode

    where ${\mathbf{x}}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = x_{1}^{\beta_{1}} \cdots x_{n}^{\beta_{n}}$, and $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_{1},\ldots, \beta_{n}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{n}$. The \textit{total degree} of a monomial $\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = x_{1}^{\beta_{1}} \ldots x_{n}^{\beta_{n}}$ is given by
    \[
        \mathrm{deg}(\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} \beta_{i} = |\boldsymbol{\beta}|.
    \relax

    Hence, the degree of $g$ is defined by
    \[
        \mathrm{deg}(g) = \mathrm{max}\{|\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mid a_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \neq 0\}.

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $f, h$ and $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}$ be polynomials in $\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ with $g_{i} \neq 0$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$. Let $G = \{g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}\}$. We say $f$ \textit{reduces} to $h$ modulo $G$, denoted 
    \[
        f \xrightarrow{\hspace{0.2cm} G \hspace{0.2cm}}_{+} h
    \relax
    \ifmmode

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    A polynomial $r$ is called \textit{reduced} with respect to a set of non-zero polynomials $G = \{g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}\}$ if $r=0$ or no power product that appears in $r$ is divisible by any one of the $\mathrm{lp}(g_{i})$, for $i=1,\ldots,k$.  That is, $r$ cannot be reduced modulo $G$.
head: environment

label: theorem-div-algo
title: Theorem
body_md:
\relax{theorem-div-algo}
    Given a set of nonzero polynomials $G = \{g_{1}, \ldots, g_{k}\}$, and a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{K}[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}],$ the Division Algorithm produces polynomials $u_{1},\ldots, u_{k}, r \in \mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ such that
    \[
        f = u_{1}g_{1} + \cdots + u_{k}g_{k} + r,
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi
    \noindent
    with $r$ reduced with respect to $G$ and 
    \[
    \mathrm{lp}(f) = \max(\max\limits_{i \in [1,k]} (\mathrm{lp}(u_{i}) \mathrm{lp}(g_{i})), \mathrm{lp}(r)).
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
    Let $G = \{g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}\}$ be a set of nonzero polynomials contained in an ideal $I$. G is called a \textit{Gröbner basis} if and only if for all $f \in I$, with $f \neq 0$, there exists an $i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ such that $\mathrm{lp}(g_{i}) \mid \mathrm{lp}(f).$

title: Definition
body_md:
\normalfont
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field. A subset $F$ that is itself a field under the operations of $\mathbb{K}$ is called a \textit{subfield} of $\mathbb{K}$. The field $\mathbb{K}$ is called an \textit{extension field} of $F$. If $F \neq \mathbb{K}$, $F$ is called a \textit{proper} subfield of $\mathbb{K}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field. The prime subfield of $\mathbb{K}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}$ if $\mathbb{K}$ has characteristic $0$, and is isomorphic to $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $\mathbb{K}$ has characteristic $p$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: We must highlight that, while we introduced Hilbert's Weak Nullstellensatz as a motivation for Section \ref{Grobner bases}, we do not require an algebraically closed field for our argument. Namely, we only justify the trivial direction $1 \in I \implies 1 \in I^{\mathbb{K}}$ such that $\mathbb{F}_{3} \subset \mathbb{K}$ and $\mathbb{K}$ is any field of characteristic 3.
head: environment

label: scalar-extensions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\relax{scalar-extensions}    
Let $F$ be a field, $I = \langle f_{1}, \ldots, f_{m} \rangle \subset F[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}]$ an ideal, and let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field extension such that $F \subset \mathbb{K}$. Define the extended ideal $I^{\mathbb{K}} \coloneqq I \cdot \mathbb{K}[x_1, \ldots, x_n] = \langle \tilde{\iota}(f_{1}), \ldots, \tilde{\iota}(f_{m}) \rangle \subset \mathbb{K}[x_1, \ldots, x_n].$ If $1 \in I$, then $1 \in I^{\mathbb{K}}$. In particular, $V_{\mathbb{K}}(I^{\mathbb{K}}) = \varnothing$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inclusion $\iota : F \hookrightarrow \mathbb{K}$ induces the injective ring homomorphism
    \[
        \tilde{\iota}: F[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}] \hookrightarrow \mathbb{K}[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}]
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi 

    \noindent
    that fixes each indeterminate and extends the coefficients. Since $1 \in I$, there exist polynomials $h_1, \ldots, h_m \in F[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}]$ such that 
    \[
        \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}h_{i}f_{i} = 1.
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    \noindent
    Applying $\tilde{\iota}$ to the previous identity yields 
    \[ 
       \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m} \tilde{\iota}(h_{i}) \tilde{\iota}(f_{i}) = 1 \in \mathbb{K}[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}].
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    \noindent
    Since each $\tilde{\iota}(f_{i}) = f_{i}$, $i=1, \ldots,m$, viewed in $\mathbb{K}[x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}]$, we have $1 \in I^{\mathbb{K}}$.

    Now, suppose that ${\bf{x}} = (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) \in \mathbb{K}^{n}$ is a common zero of $I^{\mathbb{K}}$. Then, evaluating at $\bf{x}$, we have  
    \[
      \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m} \tilde{\iota}(h_{i}({\bf{x}})) f_{i}({\bf{x}}) = 1  \implies 0=1,
    \relax
    \ifmmode
      \egroup \m@th$\hfil \egroup
      \end{trivlist} 
    \else $$
    \fi

    \noindent
    which is impossible. Therefore, no solution exists in $\mathbb{K}^{n}$ and thus $V_{\mathbb{K}}(I^{\mathbb{K}}) = \varnothing$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field of characteristic different from $2$. Then, the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$ does not admit a compatible left-symmetric superalgebra structure.
head: environment
name: Left-Symmetric Structures on $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$ admits a compatible left-symmetric superalgebra structure over $\mathbb{K}$. Then, its restriction to the even part $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar{0}}$ defines a compatible left-symmetric algebra structure on $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)_{\bar{0}} \cong \mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{K})$.

    In characteristic $0$, such a structure on $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{K})$ is ruled out by Helmstetter's standard nonexistence result for perfect Lie algebras N\noexpand\thmhead@plainN\csname cite \endcsname{helmstetter}.

    In characteristic $p >3$, Burde's result (established in Theorem \ref{burde-theorem-specialized}) rules it out because $\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{K})) = 3$ and $p$ does not divide $3$.

    It remains to consider the case of characteristic $3$. By changing the base field, the assumed left-symmetric superalgebra over $\mathbb{K}$ extends to a left-symmetric structure over the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{K}}$, with the even part remaining a left-symmetric algebra on $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{K})$. Burde classifies all compatible left-symmetric algebra structures on $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{K})$ over algebraically closed fields into the four families $\mathcal{A}_{1,u,v}$, $\mathcal{A}_{2, \gamma}$, $\mathcal{A}_{3}$, and $\mathcal{A}_{4}$. The Gröbner basis computations in Section \ref{grobner-basis-comp} show that, for each of the four structures, the resulting polynomial system is inconsistent over $\mathbb{F}_3$. Using Lemma \ref{scalar-extensions}, this inconsistency extends to any field of characteristic $3$. This includes the algebraically closed field $\overline{\mathbb{K}}$. Hence, none of the four even-part structures extends to a compatible left-symmetric superalgebra structure on $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$, thus contradicting the assumption we made earlier. Therefore, no compatible left-symmetric superalgebra structure exists on $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$ for $\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{K})$ different from $2$.
head: environment
